rights.basis: Richard Mott Gummere died on 3 December 1969. His Loeb translation appeared in three volumes, 1917, 1920 and 1925. Works published before 1 January 1931 are in the public domain in the United States. In the European Union, the United Kingdom and Turkey the general term is the translator’s life plus 70 years, counted to the end of the year, so the translation is protected there through 31 December 2039. Each of those laws also compares the term with the work’s country of origin; that comparison was not worked out. Each allows quotation of a published work with its source named, within conditions (EU Directive 2001/29/EC art. 5(3)(d); UK CDPA s.30(1ZA); Turkey Law 5846 art. 35). This is a record of facts for the owner, not legal advice.

sections.title: What I learned, and from whom

statement.t: I am a member of one body of reasoning beings, made for a shared life with them.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the two central claims gain a second author, the body picture gains an arch beside it, and the article gains a concrete act, a second exercise and a caution about crowds: I may step back from them, but I must not hate them. He disputes none of Marcus’s claims here.

articles.title: The work that belongs to me

statement.t: My work is to let reason lead in how I treat other people, in how I handle my body, and in how I judge.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, four of the five claims gain a second author, Practice gains a way to stay my own master amid business, and “When it breaks” gains what Marcus does not say in this section: to look to the reason for an action and not to its result. To the claim about the body he adds that it may still be indulged somewhat.

statement.t: Whatever happens to me, I accept it and do not complain.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca every claim gains a second author, the empty Practice label gets two exercises, “Why” gets a further argument, and “In action” gains what I may still prefer before a hardship comes. Nothing of Marcus’s is challenged.

articles.title: The reason that governs the whole

statement.t: The reason that orders the world and the reason that guides me are alike.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, four of the five claims gain a second author, the empty “When it breaks” gets its first item, “In action” says what worship of the governing power is enough, and “Why” gains a limit: its care may miss one person.

statement.t: Like everything that exists, the gods included, I am made for something, namely to use my reason, which turns toward others.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, each claim gains a second author on one of its parts, and the article gains three things Marcus leaves out here: the answer to what I was made for, what failing at it looks like, and the joy that is left when pleasure is ruled out.

articles.title: What the whole sends in its season

statement.t: What the whole brings me is good for me and comes at the right time, so I take its side.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, taking the universe’s side gains two witnesses, and the article gains what Marcus leaves out here: the hard things, paid willingly as a tax; words for a setback; a test for prayer; how to stand under pain; an answer when a death seems too early; and what holds if I doubt it. He backs nothing in the first claim, and he limits the second: he does not crave hardship itself.

articles.title: My judgment is up to me

statement.t: What troubles me rests on my judgment; that judgment is up to me, and when I take it away there is calm.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the first and the fifth claims gain a second author. Practice gains questions to put to myself and words for facing a feared event, and “when it breaks” gains where false opinions come from and how they are driven out. He limits the first claim (even pain with no opinion added is still slight) and the fourth (the mind is struck by feelings reason cannot rout), and he challenges the fifth: where all is in doubt, he would have me believe what I prefer.

articles.title: What happens can be borne and does not harm me

statement.t: Nothing happens to me that I cannot bear; what happens harms me only if I judge it bad, and it does not stop me from being good and just.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, five of the six claims gain a second witness: nothing is beyond my power to bear, I suffer according to opinion, pain is a sensation of the body, whatever I am given is material for virtue, and pain is slight when opinion adds nothing to it. The article gains a way of turning the mind from pain, a question that catches the sorrow I add myself, and a reason to go on living when I could leave. He challenges the first claim: a pain I cannot bear may come, though it is short. He limits the third: the mind is steady only once virtue is complete.

articles.title: Keeping the few names I have given myself

statement.t: I keep to the few names I have given myself, do each thing as someone about to leave life, and need no one as witness.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, five of the six claims gain a second author; only the review of my conduct does not. Practice gains a daily review with a test of steadiness, action gains a warning against making a show of plainness, and the side on what failing looks like gains what Seneca says of those who are not yet one person. He limits two claims: until I respect myself I keep a witness in mind, and a day is lived as one that might be my last, not snatched at as the last. The side on doubt stays empty.

articles.title: Living now as one about to die

statement.t: Before long I shall be no one and nowhere, so I live the present justly, as one already at the end, and wait for death cheerfully.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, living as one already at the end gains three witnesses, waiting for death gains three, and what is enough and the view from above gain one each. Practice gains a nightly exercise and the reminder that a cheerful death is long prepared; When it breaks gains a name for the failure, a life always postponed. He limits leaving the past behind, and he challenges the claim that being remembered is of no account. His allowance for ending one’s own life, which differs from waiting for the natural end, is left out of this article.

articles.title: Coming back to my principles and keeping them ready

statement.t: When I fall short of philosophy I do not give up: I do what nature asks, keep my principles at hand and look at each thing stripped bare.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, four of the five claims gain a second author: that the work needs no audience, that acting well comes from principles kept ready, that each thing is looked at bare, and that I do not give up. The article gains a measure for the learner, an image for what makes the teaching hold, a way to keep principles at hand, the same stripping used on what frightens, and what stands behind “I cannot”. He limits three claims: needing no one to see, since until I respect myself I picture a good man watching; coming back, since no one resumes where he left off; and the situation I am in, since affairs that engross me are to be put out of the way.

statement.t: At any hour I can retreat into myself, and I keep to my own mind rather than to what others say and do.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the retreat of claim 1 gains a second author for its hour and its place, the praise of claim 2 and the target of claim 6 gain one each; the practice gains a way to keep my mind within amid noise, and what failing looks like gains two signs: travelling to escape my own gloom, and starting at every sound. He sets two limits on the retreat: one goes into the statement (it is right only for someone already good), and one into claim 1 (a mind not yet sound is harmed by some places).

articles.title: Whether anything is better than virtue

statement.t: Nothing is better than the spirit within me and its virtue, and no one can prevent me from living by it.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, three claims gain a second author: the good that is my own, keeping to what is necessary, and what pulls me away from it. “Why” gains his argument that reason is a human being’s own good, and “In action” gains where the good in a choice lies. He limits the claim that no one can prevent me from living well: nothing can break the happiness of the wise, but mine can be broken off while I am short of perfection, and old age can shatter the mind.

statement.t: I live with the gods and meet their power always, revere both them and reason, and keep before me the dawn sky and a good person of old.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, claim 1 gains a second author for calling the spirit, which is reason, a fragment of the divine, and claim 3 a second author for keeping one good person in mind. The article gains what Marcus leaves out here: God as a witness within me, what worship consists in, the chosen person as a watcher, an example of what I turn back from when I return to reason, and what holds if no guardian was given to me. He limits claim 3: I need the person as a guard over me only until I respect myself.

articles.title: Blaming no one for what is not up to me

statement.t: I do not let what is not up to me make a difference to me, and I blame no one for it, neither the gods nor people.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the slavery of claim c1 and the case against the gods in claim c5 gain a second author; what I do gains philosophy turned on my own faults, the practice gains happiness without vows, and “If I doubt it” gains a second answer to the gods’ neglect. He limits two claims: the gods are sometimes unmindful of the individual, and for the harm we bring on ourselves we can complain of ourselves.

articles.title: Happiness and unhappiness are my own doing

statement.t: My happiness is decided in my own soul, and I need nothing besides; not wanting what happens, I desert nature and the law that send it.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the first claim gains two witnesses and the second one. The article gains a sentence that the editor reads as joining its two halves (being under orders does not make me unhappy; acting against my will does), the spirit within, a daily review, a way back, and an answer to an objection. He limits the second claim: the wise man is enough for a happy life, not for staying alive.

statement.t: Any moment now I may die; I live without pretence, here as anywhere, and I am ready to go.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, four claims gain a second author: that death is near, that I am ready to go, that I do not pretend, and, in claim 4, both “wherever I am” and preferring death to living another way. He adds what can serve as a reason for the article, though he does not offer it as one: death will show whether my brave words were felt or a pretence. He adds words to say each night, and he limits the readiness to die: not in haste, and not from a longing for death.

statement.t: Wherever I am put, and equally whatever is given me or taken back, a good state of soul and good actions are enough for me.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, all three claims gain a second author. For the first: any land I am driven to can be a hospitable home, the soul by its own power makes a life happy or wretched, and the real good comes from a good conscience, honourable purposes and right actions. For the second: a good man bears whatever happens to him as the result of divine law. For the third: a prayer hands to Jupiter the choice of where I am led. The article gains two grounds (the person matters more than the place; a spirit within treats me as I treat it), two things under “In action” (how to hold what is given; making something of whatever fortune I find) and a rehearsal of poverty and exile. Nothing is added under “If I doubt it”. He limits the first claim: some places harm a mind still recovering, and where he may choose he avoids them.

statement.t: Whoever wrongs me does it against their will and cannot harm me, and I teach them or bear with them.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, claims 2, 5 and 6 gain a second author. The practice gains a habit of reading words and looks generously, and the side of failing gains three things: going on giving after ingratitude, that how far anger goes depends on the soul a provocation reaches, and not copying bad people because they are many. He challenges claim 1, holding that people know what evil is and do not care, and claim 2, holding that the least part of a wrong does reach the one wronged; he limits claim 4 to those willing to listen.

articles.title: Taking a thing apart: material, cause, purpose and time

statement.t: I look at what each thing itself is, I take it apart into its material, its cause and its purpose, and I ask how long it lasts.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the division into material and cause gains a second author, and so does asking what each thing is and what it is worth. The article gains what Marcus leaves out here: why to look, since what I fear, seen as it is at bottom, holds nothing but my fear; what failing looks like; a rule that the parts must not be countless and tiny; and what holds if I cannot be certain which account of what causes things is true.

statement.t: It is up to me to keep wiping out impressions and to make every impulse with a reservation, on condition that nothing prevents it.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, claim 2 (my mind cannot be harmed) and claim 4 (impulse by worth, desire kept out) gain a second author, and the article gains how an impression leads to an act, worth, impulse and action as three steps in order, what being carried along by impulse looks like, and what to do if I leave open what is in my power. He limits claim 1: once a passion is let in, it is no longer in my power; and claim 4: keeping desire out still leaves me free to wish.

articles.title: Good whatever others say, and open to being set right

statement.t: Whatever others say of me, I act well, and I change my mind only when I am shown what is true, just or of common benefit.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, acting well while spoken ill of and wanting approval as the failure gain a second author, the ground gains a reward that lies in the deed itself, the way back gains an answer for one who cannot stand alone, and the claim that my mind stands upright by itself is limited, since he holds that no one rises above his folly unaided.

statement.t: I keep to my own reason as a doctor keeps to the craft, and attend only to what I am doing now, even when those I work for speak ill of me.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the article gains what Marcus leaves out here: a ground, that what a pilot answers for is the work and not its success; how far to go along with other people, which 6.32 says only of craftsmen; and, under “When it breaks”, philosophy that courts applause. He backs nothing in the one claim, and he limits the picture it uses: a pilot’s or a physician’s skill is for the good of other people, and the wise person’s good is their own as well.

articles.title: Training, and the use of reason

statement.t: I treat living as a skill: I learn it by training, I bring reason to it and wait for nothing else, and I use it to face what happens.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the first two claims gain a second author, the article gains two reasons under Why, an exercise of thinking ahead and three things for when it breaks, and claims 2 and 3 are limited: I need a helping hand, and I may fall so long as I rise again.

statement.t: I keep going back to myself and to philosophy, rest in philosophy and in acting as a member of a community, and toil without complaint.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, going back into myself and going to philosophy each gain a witness, and the article gains a reason not to complain, justice without reward or renown, the company of the best people of any age and what to do while I am not yet fit to be alone with myself; he limits the going back into myself, and where Marcus waits on the court he would put the affairs that take up his time out of the way.

articles.title: The morning, and the question before each action

statement.t: I get up for the work I was made for, I question each thing I do, and when I have done good I look for nothing more.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, looking for nothing after doing good gains a second author. Under Why he adds the purpose of the whole life, against which each act is weighed; under Practice, death kept in mind at lying down and at waking, so that each morning is a gift, and a review of each day; under When it breaks, owning a fault as the sign that I am awake. He limits and challenges nothing.

statement.t: Before I want anyone’s praise I look into their mind; praise makes me no better, and fame after death is nothing to me.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, three claims gain a second author: seeing what sort of people they are (claim 1), not wanting praise from people I cannot praise (claim 2), and taking others’ word for what I am (claim 4). The article gains an audience of a few, one or none; a way to weigh judgments; and a way back: what I think of myself counts for more. He challenges two claims: he holds that those who come after will judge without prejudice, and that deserved praise from good people is a good.

statement.t: A wrong harms the one who does it, not the one it is done to, so I leave another’s wrong with them.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, where the harm of a wrong lies gains a second witness and a challenge: he holds that the least and lightest part of a wrong reaches the one it is done to, and that bad people make one another worse. Practice gains forgetting wrongs on purpose and reading words and looks generously, and In action gains keeping watch against what people may do.

statement.t: I stand upright on my own, and my best way to fight back is not to become like those I fight.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the article gains what Marcus leaves out here: that a fall from a height has nothing evil in it, that a wise person’s good is shared with the people they live with, that the worst part of a wrong stays with the one who does it, that a person’s good is a free and upright mind subject to nothing, and that a slanderous companion rubs off on me and that I should not copy the bad because they are many. The article has no fused claims, so he backs none, and he limits nothing.

articles.title: The sameness and meanness of things

statement.t: Everything in life is the same as it always was and foul in what it is made of, and I am no stranger to it.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, being surprised at what happens gains a second author, and the article gains what Marcus leaves out here: what to do, which is to think ahead; what surprise costs; a way back after a loss; and words to say when wealth dazzles me. He limits the distaste for life as a whole, which must not turn into hating life, and he challenges the little breath: for him the soul is heavenly, not of one kind with dust and bones.

statement.t: Everything lies in how my soul uses itself: it can see itself and the whole, or do violence to itself.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the claims on what my soul sees, on going straight toward its end and on being ready when life ends gain a second author. Practice gains a daily review, When it breaks gains the soul that turns from king to tyrant, which also extends the statement, and If I doubt it gains a reason to fear neither end nor change. He limits the claim on what is mine: the body is to be cherished with care, though not lived for.

statement.t: All things change, and I with them; the change is the work of nature and nothing bad, and nothing that passes is great.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, five claims gain a second author: that all things change and I with them, that I look down on what passes, the practice of seeing all of time, that a loss is only a change, and that a thing is resolved into its elements. The ground gains one good that does not perish; what breaks gains the fear of a death already under way and the weariness that sameness can breed. He backs the third claim’s contempt for what passes in Letter 58 and limits it in Letter 98: what I lose I keep in memory, with thanks.

statement.t: What I am made of came out of the whole, goes back into it and is shaped again, and my ending belongs to the way I am made.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, claims 1, 2 and 3 each gain a second author, and the article gains what Marcus leaves out here: an exercise for facing death, what failing looks like and the way back, and what holds if death is simply the end. He limits claim 4: death is no evil, but it keeps a look of evil.

statement.t: I keep in mind that all before me, the greatest too, are dead and soon forgotten, and I put my effort into living justly.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, four claims gain a second author: that everyone dies, that those who outlive me follow, that death is a harbour, and what death may be. The action side gains an answer to the objection that my own deed will be forgotten or little thanked, the practice side gains thinking of my own death beside the deaths of those I love, and the claim about fame is challenged: he holds that whatever fame virtue earns does not pass away.

articles.title: The length of a life and the use of its time

statement.t: How long I live does not matter; my time has a limit, and I hurry to become good while it is still possible.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, four of the five claims gain a second author: young and old alike are short-lived beside eternity, a limit is fixed and life is taken a little each day, I hasten, and while I postpone, life speeds by. In action, Practice and If I doubt it each gain something Marcus does not say here, and claim 5 is limited: age need not harm the mind, though Seneca also says that wisdom is hard to learn when old.

statement.t: My death is nature’s work, like the passing of my ages before it, so I go graciously and leave the people of my life kindly.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the ages of a life gain a second author. Practice gains a daily rehearsal, When it breaks gains the longing for death, and If I doubt it gains what remains of me either way. He limits claim 3, since death keeps a look of evil, and claim 5, since those I hold dear can be a reason to stay.

articles.title: What I learned, and from whom

statement.t: I live as the people who brought me up and taught me showed me: even-tempered, careful in what I believe, and needing little.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, freedom from anger, steadiness in illness, slowness to believe and easy reconciliation each gain a second author. The article gains a reason for learning from people, what happens when a teacher’s habit is broken, and what holds if a teacher was wrong. He limits the training in hardness: a few days at a time, as a test, not a penance or a show.

statement.t: I measure a person by the soul, not by fame or power: a soul that is just, and for which dying is not the worst thing.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, four of the six claims gain a second author: that staying alive is not the great thing, that the soul is the measure and fame is not, that being just is enough, and the wide view. The article gains a way to look at a person stripped of everything but the soul, a model to live by, birth set beside fame and power, the names of what the conquerors were slaves to, justice without renown, and the duty to stay alive for those who need me. He limits one claim: for him the glory of a death proves nothing, but how a person meets death does judge a soul.
